explanation:
[FEATURE: hr]
[EFFECT] The hour of the day has a strongly non-monotonic, double-peaked effect. Demand is at its lowest in the very early morning (around 4 a.m., contribution ≈ −3.2 in log space), climbs sharply from 5 a.m. onward, reaches a first peak at 8 a.m. (contribution ≈ +0.54), dips slightly in mid-morning, then surges to its highest point at 5 p.m. (contribution ≈ +0.80), before falling steadily back to near-zero by midnight.
[IMPORTANCE] This is by far the strongest feature in the model (rank 1, importance 0.83) — roughly four times more influential than the next feature. Getting the time-of-day pattern right is the single biggest driver of the model's predictions.

---

[FEATURE: temp]
[EFFECT] Temperature has a non-monotonic (inverted-U) effect. Very cold conditions (normalised temp ≈ 0.02–0.10, i.e. roughly 1–4 °C) strongly suppress demand (contribution around −0.75 to −0.82). As temperature rises, demand increases steeply, peaking at a normalised value of about 0.70–0.74 (roughly 29–30 °C, contribution ≈ +0.17). Above that sweet spot, very high temperatures begin to pull demand back down, with the hottest readings (≈ 41 °C) returning to negative territory (contribution ≈ −0.23).
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 3 (importance 0.197), nearly tied with yr — one of the three most influential features in the model.

---

[FEATURE: yr]
[EFFECT] Year acts as a simple step change: 2011 reduces predicted demand (contribution ≈ −0.23) while 2012 boosts it (contribution ≈ +0.17), reflecting overall growth in the bike-share system over time.
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 2 (importance 0.200), just ahead of temperature — the second most influential feature, capturing the year-on-year growth trend.

---

[FEATURE: mnth]
[EFFECT] Month shows a broadly rising-then-plateauing pattern across the year. January has the strongest negative pull (contribution ≈ −0.34) and demand builds through spring, plateauing across summer and early autumn with September being the highest month (contribution ≈ +0.12). December dips slightly back to near-neutral (−0.03).
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 5 (importance 0.118), a moderate contributor — meaningful for seasonal planning but well below hour, year, and temperature.

---

[FEATURE: hum]
[EFFECT] Humidity has a non-monotonic effect with a gentle plateau in the middle and a sharp drop at the high end. At moderate humidity levels (roughly 20–55%, normalised 0.20–0.55), the contribution is mildly positive (up to about +0.09). Once humidity climbs above about 75% (normalised ≈ 0.75), the effect turns increasingly negative, reaching around −0.30 at 100% humidity. Extremely low humidity (near 0%) is also slightly negative, but those conditions are rare.
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 6 (importance 0.077) — a noticeable but secondary weather factor, roughly half the influence of month.

---

[FEATURE: weathersit]
[EFFECT] Weather situation has a categorical step-down pattern. Clear skies (category 1) provide a small boost (contribution ≈ +0.03); mist or cloud (category 2) is nearly neutral (−0.01); light rain or snow (category 3) causes a substantial drop in predicted demand (contribution ≈ −0.33); heavy rain (category 4) is also negative (−0.17), though its estimate is based on very few hours in the data.
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 7 (importance 0.051) — a real but modest effect, roughly a quarter the size of temperature.

---

[FEATURE: weekday]
[EFFECT] Weekday shows a gradual upward trend from Sunday through Friday, with a slight dip on Saturday relative to Friday. Sunday and Monday have the most negative mean contributions (around −0.08 and −0.07), mid-week days are mildly negative (−0.06 to −0.02), while Friday and Saturday are lightly positive (+0.03 and +0.01). The overall range of mean contributions is small (about 0.10 log units), though within each day the model captures wide variation driven by other features like hour.
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 4 (importance 0.173) — the fourth most important feature, reflecting differences in usage patterns across the week, though individual hours matter far more within any given day.

---

[FEATURE: windspeed]
[EFFECT] Wind speed has a mostly negative and roughly monotonic effect once winds rise above a low threshold. At low wind speeds (up to roughly 17 km/h, normalised ≈ 0.25), the contribution is near-neutral to very slightly positive. Above that, higher wind speeds progressively lower predicted demand, reaching around −0.14 to −0.69 at the strongest winds recorded.
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 8 (importance 0.020) — a minor feature with a real directional signal but small overall influence compared to the features above it.

---

[FEATURE: holiday]
[EFFECT] Holiday is a simple two-value step: non-holiday hours have a contribution of essentially zero (+0.001), while holiday hours carry a negative contribution of about −0.17, meaning the model predicts noticeably fewer rentals on public holidays than on ordinary days.
[IMPORTANCE] Rank 9 (importance 0.012) — the least influential feature in the model; its effect is real but small and can be considered a minor correction rather than a primary driver.

---

[RECOMMENDATION] Hour of the day and temperature are overwhelmingly the strongest demand drivers, so staffing and bike redistribution plans should first be built around the two daily rush-hour peaks (morning around 8 a.m. and evening around 5 p.m.) and then adjusted upward or downward based on the day's forecast temperature — scaling up resources for mild, warm days and scaling back for very cold or very hot conditions.
